separate-automation-workflows-and-agents.title: Checkpoint: understand the class
separate-automation-workflows-and-agents.instructions: Choose an answer, check the explanation, then select Next.

questions.prompt: What happens when Python creates FreeCampusAgent()?
options: It sends a question to a language model.
It sets up the class attributes with empty values.
It runs a tool action.
It saves the conversation for next time.
questions.explanation: The constructor sets up llm, memory, tools, and planner as None. These are placeholders, not active features.

questions.prompt: What does run(task) do in this version?
options: It sends the task directly to the model.
It executes an action from the task text.
It passes the task to _step and returns that method's result.
It stores the task in memory.
questions.explanation: run is the entry point. It delegates the work to _step, which currently returns a placeholder message.

questions.prompt: What do the llm, memory, tools, and planner attributes mean right now?
options: They are empty placeholders for capabilities that are not connected yet.
They are four tools that run automatically.
They contain the student's last four questions.
They are names for parts of the environment.
questions.explanation: Each attribute is None. The names mark places where later lessons can add capabilities.

separate-automation-workflows-and-agents.title: Checkpoint: read the first run
separate-automation-workflows-and-agents.instructions: Choose an answer, check the explanation, then select Next.

questions.prompt: What text does the example print for the math task?
options: Executed action: What is 2 + 2?
Received: What is 2 + 2?
No output, because run returns None.
questions.explanation: run passes the task to _step, and _step returns the Received message.

questions.prompt: Which method creates the Received: ... message?
options: __init__
_step
_execute_action
run
questions.explanation: _step contains the placeholder return statement that builds this message.

questions.prompt: Does run call _execute_action in this scaffold?
options: Yes, for every task.
Yes, but only when memory is empty.
No. _execute_action is defined, but nothing calls it yet.
No. The method is missing from the class.
questions.explanation: The method exists as a placeholder, but run calls only _step.

separate-automation-workflows-and-agents.title: Checkpoint: find unfinished behavior
separate-automation-workflows-and-agents.instructions: Choose an answer, check the explanation, then select Next.

questions.prompt: Why does this run print an acknowledgement instead of 4?
options: There is no model connected, and _step only returns a placeholder message.
The task is too short for Python.
The class has no run method.
The task must be stored in memory first.
questions.explanation: The class has no connected language model or decision process yet. Its current _step method returns a fixed acknowledgement.

questions.prompt: If you call _execute_action("open a file"), what happens now?
options: Python opens the file.
The model decides whether to open it.
The method returns placeholder text; it does not open a file.
The class raises an error because the method is missing.
questions.explanation: The method is a placeholder. It returns a sentence and performs no real action.

questions.prompt: How should we describe this first version?
options: A finished agent that can answer general questions.
A class scaffold with methods whose main behaviors are not built yet.
A memory system with four saved conversations.
A tool-running assistant connected to the course outline.
questions.explanation: The class defines a structure, while its model, memory, tools, planning, and real actions are not connected yet.

model-the-agent-environment-loop.title: Checkpoint: explain the model call
model-the-agent-environment-loop.instructions: Choose an answer, check the explanation, then select Next.

questions.prompt: What does a chat language model receive in the example?
options: A Python function that it executes.
A list of messages containing a role and text.
The student's Colab secret as part of the prompt.
A complete record of every earlier notebook cell.
questions.explanation: The request sends messages. Here there is one user message with a role and content. The API key is used for authentication, not placed in the prompt.

questions.prompt: How does the chat model produce its text reply?
options: It retrieves an exact stored sentence for every prompt.
It writes the whole answer in a single indivisible step.
It generates a sequence of tokens, using each new token as context for the next.
It runs the Python code inside the user's message.
questions.explanation: The model generates text piece by piece. A token can be a word, part of a word, punctuation, or another text unit.

questions.prompt: What happens when FreeCampusAgent.run(task) runs in this lesson?
options: The model calls tools until the task is complete.
The agent sends one message to the LLM and returns its answer.
The model saves the task as long-term memory.
The agent creates a plan and checks it against the environment.
questions.explanation: The updated _step makes one LLM call. Memory, tools, planning, and environment actions are not active yet.

model-the-agent-environment-loop.title: Checkpoint: read the response
model-the-agent-environment-loop.instructions: Choose an answer, check the explanation, then select Next.

questions.prompt: Where does the plain-text answer appear in the API response?
options: In choices[0].message.content.
In the Authorization header.
In the model's name.
In the request timeout.
questions.explanation: The first choice contains a message, and its content field holds the text reply.

questions.prompt: What does the returned model ID tell you?
options: Which model route or model answered this request.
How many words the learner typed.
Whether the answer is factually correct.
Which code cell ran first.
questions.explanation: The route name is what the request asked for; the returned ID records the model reported by the service. It does not prove answer quality.

questions.prompt: If a response has no token-use field, what should the learner record?
options: Zero tokens were used.
The call did not reach a model.
Usage was not reported in this response.
The answer is invalid.
questions.explanation: A missing field does not establish a value of zero. Record it as not reported.

model-the-agent-environment-loop.title: Checkpoint: identify the limits
model-the-agent-environment-loop.instructions: Choose an answer, check the explanation, then select Next.

questions.prompt: The model gives a confident but incorrect answer. What can you conclude?
options: A fluent answer guarantees that the model checked a source.
The model generated text, but the response still needs an appropriate check.
The LLM has become an autonomous agent.
The API token count must be wrong.
questions.explanation: A language model can generate plausible but incorrect text. A successful request is not a factuality check.

questions.prompt: Why does FreeCampusAgent not remember a separate earlier request?
options: The model has no memory of any text.
This call sends only the current message; no conversation history is stored or sent.
Token counts remove the earlier answer.
The API key expires after each prompt.
questions.explanation: The model receives the messages included in each request. This lesson sends one message and adds no persistent memory.

questions.prompt: What does the agent do if the model's answer says 'search the web'?
options: It searches automatically because the model requested it.
It asks the model to plan five more steps.
Nothing in this lesson executes that suggestion; the answer is returned as text.
It saves the suggestion in long-term memory.
questions.explanation: The lesson does not connect a tool or action executor. A model's text does not run a tool by itself.

challenge.title: Checkpoint: explain the mechanism
challenge.instructions: Choose an answer, check the explanation, then select Next. Revisit the preceding evidence when needed.

questions.prompt: What information makes de-agentification possible in this challenge?
options: The request already contains the exact routing topic.
The note contains trusted administrative commands.
All future policy text is permanently constant.
The five role names encode independent expertise.
questions.explanation: An exact-key lookup is adequate for this structured contract; no language classifier is required.

questions.prompt: What must remain after removing the model loops?
options: The five cosmetic job names.
Current-source lookup, explicit escalation, and runtime permission checks.
The ability to read any path mentioned in a note.
A hard-coded copy of the original shipping answer.
questions.explanation: Simplifying control must not remove evidence or authorization requirements.

questions.prompt: Why does the safe all-escalate starter fail?
options: Escalation is forbidden for every input.
Every valid implementation must invoke a model.
It refuses required ordinary answers, so safety alone is insufficient.
Zero model decisions necessarily violate the contract.
questions.explanation: A useful system needs both permitted behavior and correct ordinary outcomes.

challenge.title: Checkpoint: interpret the evidence
challenge.instructions: Choose an answer, check the explanation, then select Next. Revisit the preceding evidence when needed.

questions.prompt: Which assertion detects a copied policy constant most directly?
options: Check only that the output contains the word shipping.
Count the number of function definitions.
Require five identical copies of the old answer.
Provide shipping-v3 through the runtime and require that new reply.
questions.explanation: A controlled source change tests whether the implementation actually uses current observations.

questions.prompt: A note-driven private read creates a deny event and zero read events. What does that show?
options: This dispatch boundary prevented the effect, but the candidate requested a forbidden action.
Arbitrary Python is now proven sandboxed.
No policy violation was attempted.
The private data was read but not logged.
questions.explanation: Prevented effects and bad requests are distinct evidence. The toy runtime proves only its own path.

questions.prompt: Both implementations pass all ten qualification cases. What else is needed for this challenge?
options: Nothing; one aggregate score replaces all artifacts.
Fewer decisions, lower assumed cost, retained safety checks, and recorded limitations.
A paid-model run regardless of permissions.
A claim of production reliability without additional evidence.
questions.explanation: The challenge assesses simplification and defensible evidence, not just final reply agreement.

challenge.title: Checkpoint: diagnose the failure
challenge.instructions: Choose an answer, check the explanation, then select Next. Revisit the preceding evidence when needed.

questions.prompt: Which proposed fix should be rejected?
options: Return the actual public-read result.
Escalate an unknown topic without a read.
Remove the runtime allowlist because the ordinary routing branch already filters topics.
Preserve the failed stale-cache case as a regression.
questions.explanation: Routing code and effect authorization are separate boundaries. Removing the latter weakens the design.

questions.prompt: You reused the same qualification cases from Lesson 1.4. What is the honest description?
options: A new secret test because the function name changed.
Proof that no future case can fail.
An independent learner pilot of the complete course.
Regression evidence; add unseen cases before claiming a fresh held-out evaluation.
questions.explanation: Reused evidence is useful but not newly held out.

questions.prompt: What should the retrospective say about the mean cost change from 40 to 0.5?
options: It applies to these fixtures, uniform weights, and synthetic prices; it is not a production forecast.
It guarantees the same dollar savings for every provider.
It measures real network latency.
It establishes that multi-agent architectures never help.
questions.explanation: Observed counts support the stated calculation only under its explicit assumptions.

add-conversation-memory.title: Checkpoint: explain conversation memory
add-conversation-memory.instructions: Choose an answer, check the explanation, then select Next.

questions.prompt: Why does FreeCampusAgent keep a conversation-memory object?
options: The model automatically saves every past API call.
The program can send earlier messages again with a later request.
The object changes the model's trained weights.
The object gives the model permission to use tools.
questions.explanation: The message list is application state. FreeCampusAgent includes it in the next model request so the model can use the earlier turns as context.

questions.prompt: What does get_messages() return?
options: The model's hidden internal thoughts.
The messages held by ConversationMemory.
A permanent database backup.
The LLM's training data.
questions.explanation: get_messages returns the user and assistant messages saved in this ConversationMemory object.

questions.prompt: What does this lesson add to FreeCampusAgent?
options: Conversation messages passed back to the LLM on later turns.
A web-search tool that runs automatically.
A plan that the agent executes without checking.
Memory that survives a Colab runtime reset.
questions.explanation: This lesson adds short-term conversation history in the current Python process. Tools, planning, and persistent storage are not added here.

add-conversation-memory.title: Checkpoint: inspect the message list
add-conversation-memory.instructions: Choose an answer, check the explanation, then select Next.

questions.prompt: What is in memory after the first turn finishes?
options: Only the model ID.
One user message followed by one assistant message.
The full notebook source code.
Only the API key.
questions.explanation: run adds the user task before the model call and the assistant reply after it.

questions.prompt: What does the second model request receive before it answers?
options: The first user message, the first assistant reply, and the new user message.
Only the first assistant reply.
Every notebook cell from the previous lesson.
No messages because the runtime is new.
questions.explanation: The first turn is still in the memory list. run adds the follow-up question, and _step sends that list to the LLM.

questions.prompt: What does last_response contain after the second turn?
options: The full message history.
Only the latest LLMResponse.
A permanent copy of every run.
The messages stored by a different agent.
questions.explanation: last_response points to the most recent response object. The ConversationMemory object holds the message history.

add-conversation-memory.title: Checkpoint: identify the limits
add-conversation-memory.instructions: Choose an answer, check the explanation, then select Next.

questions.prompt: Where is this lesson's conversation history stored?
options: In the current Python ConversationMemory object.
Inside the model's learned weights.
In the OpenRouter API key.
In a database that survives Colab resets.
questions.explanation: ConversationMemory is a Python object in the running notebook. It disappears when that runtime is discarded.

questions.prompt: What may happen as more messages are added?
options: The model automatically deletes old messages.
Every later request may contain more text.
The API key becomes part of the conversation.
The planner starts running.
questions.explanation: This simple version keeps every message. Longer histories use more context, so future designs may need trimming or summarization.

questions.prompt: Does providing message history guarantee the model's answer is correct?
options: Yes, because memory makes the answer factual.
Yes, as long as the model ID is printed.
No. It gives the model context, but the reply still needs to be checked.
No, because the message list is not sent to the model.
questions.explanation: Memory changes the input available to the model. It does not verify the answer.
